02.r: Turns from the man's expectation to Peter's reply.

03.n: Abbott-Smith explains the name as 'a stone'.

04.r: Silver, here as money the man might have hoped to receive.
04.n: Abbott-Smith gives the proper sense as 'a piece of silver', and in the New Testament both 'silver' and 'money'; he files this verse under 'silver'. This study renders it 'silver' throughout, so that it stays distinct from other words for money.

05.r: Joins the two metals; after the negative, neither one.

06.r: Gold, the other metal used for money.
06.n: Abbott-Smith calls it a diminutive of χρυσός, gold, and gives 'a piece of gold, gold'; he also records a use 'of gold coin, money'. Paired with silver here, coin is the likely sense, an inference.

08.r: Peter has no money to give.
08.n: Literally 'silver and gold is not to me'. The verb is a fuller verb for 'to be', which Abbott-Smith gives in the sense 'to be in existence, be at hand'; with a dative of the person it amounts to 'have'.

09.r: Peter is the one who has none.

10.r: Points to what Peter does have to give.

11.r: Sets what he has against what he lacks.

12.r: A different verb from the one used for the money he lacks.
12.n: The plain verb 'to have', set against the 'is not to me' of the silver and gold.

13.r: Picks up 'what I have' with emphasis: this, I give.

14.r: The man Peter is speaking to.

15.r: Peter gives at once what he has.
15.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to give', in various senses: bestow, grant, supply. A present tense: the gift happens as he speaks.

16.r: The command is spoken on Jesus' authority.

17.r: The one name in which he acts.

18.r: The name stands for the person and his authority.
18.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is the name by which a person or thing is called. That 'in the name' here means acting on his authority is a reasonable reading of the context.

20.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from χρίω, to anoint; as an adjective it means 'anointed', and in the Septuagint it stands for Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ.

22.r: Identifies which Jesus: the one from Nazareth.
22.n: Abbott-Smith: 'a Nazarene', and he cites this verse. All six translations render it 'of Nazareth'.

23.r: A command to the man to get to his feet.
23.n: Abbott-Smith notes that this imperative form is used intransitively, 'rise'. The ASV has only 'walk'; a likely reason, not confirmed here, is that its Greek text lacked 'rise up and'.

25.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to walk'. A present imperative, which the YLT brings out with 'be walking': go on walking.

tr_note: Where our text has ἔγειρε, 'rise', the Textus Receptus has ἔγειραι, another form of the same verb. The KJV's 'rise up' takes it as a command, so the English is the same either way.
